into one batched StorageView, decode all in a single batched generate call
with one prompt per window, and join the texts. This recovers the deleted
tail of every multi-minute 0715 call, which should sharply cut deletion-driven
CER versus the 30s-only stub.

capability_investigated:
generate()'s returned sequences_ids when <|notimestamps|> is removed from the
prompt — i.e. whether the decoder emits timestamp tokens and what they encode

what_i_learned:
Without <|notimestamps|> the decode emits timestamp tokens (ids >= the
<|0.00|> token id) interleaved with text tokens in sequences_ids. The last
such token gives the chunk-relative time (steps * 0.02s) the model accounted
for, so the window can advance to a model-chosen boundary instead of a fixed
30s cut. This is a return value we were throwing away by forcing notimestamps.

seek: decode each window with timestamps on, append the text tokens (filtered
below timestamp_begin), and advance seek by the last emitted timestamp
(capped at chunk length, floored at 1s for progress). Utterances split across
hard 30s boundaries should be recovered, lifting length_ratio and cutting the
dominant deletion mass.

libctranslate2.so.4 requires. ctypes.CDLL(<system libstdc++>, RTLD_GLOBAL)
run BEFORE the frozen import is the in-process LD_PRELOAD equivalent — it
publishes the missing versioned symbols into global scope so the later
ctranslate2 load resolves. Scanning the standard distro paths
(/usr/lib/x86_64-linux-gnu, /lib/x86_64-linux-gnu, /usr/lib64, /usr/lib)
and breaking on the first that loads is more robust than a single hardcoded
path. This loads a C runtime library, not a Python backend module, so it
imports neither ctranslate2 nor transformers — contract intact.

Not a decode kwarg — the module-load import ordering in transcribe.py. The
iter-56 repair tried ctypes.CDLL(<system libstdc++>, RTLD_GLOBAL) to supply
the GLIBCXX_3.4.32 node the anaconda libstdc++ lacks, but placed the preload

preload itself, is why it still resolved to anaconda's libstdc++.
what_i_learned:
The dynamic linker dedups shared objects by soname (libstdc++.so.6): once an
earlier import (numpy and its deps) pulls anaconda's libstdc++ into the
process, a later ctypes.CDLL of a system-path libstdc++.so.6 returns the
ALREADY-LOADED anaconda handle and adds no new versioned symbols — exactly
why the iter-56 traceback still names anaconda's copy. The preload can only
win the soname binding if it runs BEFORE numpy/frozen are imported, while no
libstdc++ is yet loaded. So the fix is ordering, not a new mechanism.
hypothesis:
Move the libstdc++ preload loop to the very top of the module — right after
`import ctypes`, before `import numpy as np` and the frozen import — so the
system libstdc++ carrying GLIBCXX_3.4.32 is bound to the soname first and is
in global scope when ctranslate2 loads, instead of being deduped away after
numpy has already claimed anaconda's copy.
